"API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- vercel:ai-architect: Specializes in architecting AI-powered applications on Vercel — choosing between AI SDK patterns, configuring providers, building agents, setting up durable workflows, and integrating MCP servers. Use when designing AI features, building chatbots, or creating agentic applications. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:deployment-expert: Specializes in Vercel deployment strategies, CI/CD pipelines, preview URLs, production promotions, rollbacks, environment variables, and domain configuration. Use when troubleshooting deployments, setting up CI/CD, or optimizing the deploy pipeline. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:performance-optimizer: Specializes in optimizing Vercel application performance — Core Web Vitals, rendering strategies, caching, image optimization, font loading, edge computing, and bundle size. Use when investigating slow pages, improving Lighthouse scores, or optimizing loading performance. (Tools: All tools)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- code-quality: Audit recently changed or specified files for code quality issues — naming, circular imports, TypeScript coverage, test/story existence, and structural debt. Read-only. Use after implementing a feature or before opening a PR.
- code-review: AI-powered code review using CodeRabbit. Default code-review skill. Trigger for any explicit review request AND autonomously when the agent thinks a review is needed (code/PR/quality/security).
- contentful-register-component: Register a Zimmermann React component with Contentful Studio Experiences. Use when a developer asks to register, add, or expose a React component to Contentful, or when they need to create a Contentful component definition for an existing component.
- feature-spec: Turn a plain-English feature request into a scoped implementation plan before any code is written. Asks one clarifying question at a time, then produces a spec Claude Code can execute safely. Use this before starting any non-trivial implementation session.
- generate-changelog: Generate a release changelog from conventional commits and upstream baseline notes. Produces audience-specific outputs for the dev team, QA, product, and GitHub Release. Use before cutting a release branch or when preparing release notes.
- new-component: Scaffold a new Zimmermann component under overrides/app/components/ — TypeScript, Chakra-first, with a paired Storybook story. Use whenever a new custom component is needed.
- onboarding: Interactive onboarding for new developers and QA engineers joining the Zimmermann PWA Kit project. Asks role at the start, checks the mechanical setup items, then orients the person to the rules and tools relevant to their role and squad. Run this in the first Claude Code session on a new machine or a first day on the project.
- pr-checklist: Generate a PR description and merge checklist based on the files changed on the current branch. Pairs with /code-quality.
- project-init: One-time project setup walkthrough. Runs the state detection script, fixes automatable items, asks one question at a time for human-input items, and updates the 7.1c CI/CD & Environment Setup Checklist Confluence page as each item is confirmed. Run this once when setting up the project for the first time, or when returning to check setup status.

- scope-check: Review a proposed Claude Code prompt for scope safety before it runs. Classifies every likely-touched file by tier and verdicts the prompt SAFE / RISKY / BLOCKED, rewriting it when needed.
- session-start: Run the mandatory session start ritual — reads tracking docs, runs branch + health checks, states current position. Use at the start of every coding session.
- upstream-sync-review: Review the release notes / changelog for a new @salesforce/retail-react-app version before bumping. Lightweight policy — see .docs/upstreamPolicy.md.
- agent-sdk-dev:new-sdk-app: Create and setup a new Claude Agent SDK application

- code-review:code-review: Code review a pull request

- claude-code-setup:claude-automation-recommender: Analyze a codebase and recommend Claude Code automations (hooks, subagents, skills, plugins, MCP servers). Use when user asks for automation recommendations, wants to optimize their Claude Code setup, mentions improving Claude Code workflows, asks how to first set up Claude Code for a project, or wants to know what Claude Code features they should use.
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- figma:figma-code-connect: Creates and maintains Figma Code Connect template files that map Figma components to code snippets. Use when the user mentions Code Connect, Figma component mapping, design-to-code translation, or asks to create/update .figma.ts or .figma.js files.
- figma:figma-create-new-file: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call. NEVER call `create_new_file` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Usage — /figma-create-new-file [editorType] [fileName] (e.g. /figma-create-new-file figjam My Whiteboard, /figma-create-new-file slides Q3 Review)
- figma:figma-design-to-code: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE calling the `get_design_context` Figma MCP tool. You MUST trigger this skill whenever the user wants to implement, build, port, or code up a Figma design as code. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.
- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).
- figma:figma-generate-library: Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.
- figma:figma-implement-motion: Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. Use when implementing animation/motion from a Figma design — user mentions "implement this motion", "add animation from Figma", "animate this component", provides a Figma URL whose node is animated, or when `get_design_context` returns motion data or instructs you to call `get_motion_context`.
- figma:figma-swiftui: SwiftUI ↔ Figma translation. Use whenever the user mentions Swift, SwiftUI, iOS, iPhone, or iPad — in EITHER direction — translating a Figma design into SwiftUI (design → code), or pushing SwiftUI views / screens / tokens back into a Figma file (code → design). Triggers on phrases like 'implement this Figma design in SwiftUI', 'build this screen in Swift', 'push this SwiftUI view to Figma', 'mirror my Swift code in a Figma file', or whenever a Figma URL appears alongside `.swift` files / an `.xcodeproj`. Routes to a direction-specific reference doc; loads alongside `figma-use` for the code → design path.
- figma:figma-use: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `use_figma` tool call. NEVER call `use_figma` directly without loading this skill first. Skipping it causes common, hard-to-debug failures. Trigger whenever the user wants to perform a write action or a unique read action that requires JavaScript execution in the Figma file context — e.g. create/edit/delete nodes, set up variables or tokens, build components and variants, modify auto-layout or fills, bind variables to properties, or inspect file structure programmatically.

- figma:figma-use-motion: Motion / animation context for the `use_figma` MCP tool — animating Figma nodes via manual keyframes, animation styles, easing, and timeline duration. Load alongside figma-use whenever a task involves adding, editing, or inspecting animation on a node.
- figma:figma-use-slides: This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the Slides context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.

1	# Architecture
2	
3	_Key technical decisions, stack overview, overrides pattern, component organisation, and key paths. Update this file when the stack changes, a new integration is added, or a structural decision is made._
4	
5	Production storefront for www.zimmermann.com — multi-locale, multi-currency, eight storefronts across six regions (AU, US, UK, EU, HK, ME), with both EU and US each split into two storefronts (domestic + international).
6	
7	## Pre-Build Decisions
8	
9	These decisions affect tooling, CI, and code shape that's hard to retrofit later. Status as of 2026-05-29.
10	
11	| #   | Decision                     | Status                                 |
12	| --- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
13	| 1   | Browser & device matrix      | ✅ Confirmed (informal)                |
14	| 2   | Accessibility manual testing | 🟡 Partial — vendor info pending       |
15	| 3   | Performance budgets          | ✅ Confirmed (informal)                |
16	| 4   | Client-side error reporting  | ⚪ Accepted risk — no tool             |
17	| 5   | Feature-flag tool            | ⚪ Accepted risk — Optimizely Web only |
18	| 6   | Translation fallback chain   | 🟡 Partial — Brand/Legal pending       |
19	
20	### #1 — Browser & device matrix ✅
21	
22	**Mobile perf-test floor:** current OS version −2 on iPhone and Android (iOS 17+, Android 14+), verified via BrowserStack Automate. `package.json` browserslist aligned to match.
23	**Desktop matrix** ([.browserstack.yml](../../.browserstack.yml)): Chrome + Safari (macOS Sonoma), Firefox + Edge (Windows 11) — all latest.
24	
25	### #2 — Accessibility 🟡
26	
27	**Target:** WCAG 2.2 AA, at least 2.1 AA. **Automated:** axe-core in Vitest + Playwright; Storybook a11y addon; Lighthouse CI a11y ≥0.90 ([lighthouserc.js](../../lighthouserc.js)). **Manual:** client's existing a11y vendor.
28	**Pending:** vendor name, screen-reader/browser matrix, audit cadence, remediation owner.
29	
30	### #3 — Performance budgets ✅
31	
32	**Client-mandated:** **LCP ≤ 2s** at p75 mobile, plus Lighthouse Performance ≥ 0.80, Accessibility ≥ 0.90, Best Practices ≥ 0.90. These are the only performance numbers in the signed TSD (§9).
33	**Other CWV (internal working defaults, not client-mandated):** INP ≤ 200ms · CLS ≤ 0.1. Lighthouse mobile defaults at p75.
34	**CI gate (SIT gate):** Lighthouse CI (`@lhci/cli`) asserts the Lighthouse score floors above, plus a >5pt trend-drop gate (LHCI server required). SEO intentionally not asserted. Runs on every PR to `develop` ([`digital-sit.yml`](../../.github/workflows/digital-sit.yml)), deploys to the **Dev** tier on merge — treat its numbers as a **regression indicator**, not the contractual measurement.
35	**Contractual measurement:** Client-mandated LCP and Lighthouse numbers are validated on **Stage** — the prod-mimicking tier (same MRT bundle size class, same CDN/edge configuration, same SFCC realm tier as production). The Dev tier is slower and further from the edge, so its absolute numbers will be worse — that is expected and not a sign-off concern. Full environment topology in [tsd-architecture.md §14.1](./temp/tsd-architecture.md).
36	**Bundle ceilings — internal CI policy, NOT client requirements:** `main.js` 180 kB · `vendor.js` 250 kB · `main.css` 50 kB (`bundlesize` in `package.json`). (These were set as aspirational targets early in the project. As of the last measurement the actual sizes are well above these ceilings (`main.js` ~352 kB, `vendor.js` ~2 MB) before any optimisation pass — the ceilings need to be re-baselined against measured size + a growth-only headroom (e.g. current + 10–15%) once a baseline pass is done.) Their purpose is regression detection, not a client-facing commitment.
37	**Third-party script weight:** uncapped — tight LCP is the de-facto constraint. See AGENTS.md > Performance for the deferral rule.
38	
39	### #6 — Translation fallback 🟡
40	
41	[regional.md](./prd/regional.md) REG-046: "English is the site-wide fallback." Doesn't disambiguate `en-eu` vs `en`, nor split by content type.
42	**Pending Brand/Legal decision** on the rule per content type:
43	
44	| Content type | Suggested chain          | Why                                          |
45	| ------------ | ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
46	| UI strings   | `fr-eu` → `en-eu` → `en` | Universal meaning                            |
47	| Editorial    | `fr-eu` → `en-eu` → hide | Avoid half-translated pages                  |
48	| Product copy | `fr-eu` → `en-eu` → hide | Care/sizing are region-specific (regulatory) |
49	
50	REG-047 (Contentful↔Transperfect↔SFCC workflow) remains separately TBC.
51	
52	### Accepted risks
53	
54	**#4 — No client-side error reporting.** JS errors in customer browsers (e.g. Adyen iframe failure on a specific iOS Safari version) are invisible to the team; detection relies on support tickets. Revisit post-launch if checkout completion dips unexplained.
55	
56	**#5 — No feature-flag tool.** Optimizely Web Experimentation ([analytics.md](./prd/analytics.md) AAB-004) covers analytics A/B. Note (confirmed 09-06): Optimizely is **not** a GTM tag — the PWA loads its script directly in the page head (US storefront only, single snippet across environments, before render to avoid flicker), Didomi-gated. Progressive rollout, social login dark-launch, and August-2026 payment-method gating will be handled via deploy timing and branch merges — no instant kill-switch, no % rollouts.
57	
58	## Frontend Stack
59	
60	### Bundled by PWA Kit
61	
62	| Layer                        | Library                                               | Notes                                                                                 |
63	| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
64	| Base framework               | PWA Kit v3+                                           | Salesforce storefront foundation                                                      |
65	| UI framework                 | React 18 + Chakra UI                                  | Component library + theme system                                                      |
66	| Routing                      | React Router v6                                       |                                                                                       |
67	| Server/async state           | TanStack Query (via `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react`) | All SFCC data fetching                                                                |
68	| i18n                         | react-intl                                            | Translations in `translations/`                                                       |
69	| Build + dev server           | Webpack 5 (via `pwa-kit-dev`)                         |                                                                                       |
70	| Build + test runner (legacy) | Jest (via `pwa-kit-dev test`)                         | `jest.config.js` — kept for PWA Kit internals; superseded by Vitest for project tests |
71	
72	### Project additions
73	
74	| Layer                                  | Library                                        | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
75	| -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
76	| Type safety                            | TypeScript strict mode                         | `tsconfig.json`                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
77	| Component explorer + interaction tests | Storybook 8                                    | `storybook dev -p 6006`; `play` functions are the primary tool for component-level interaction testing                                                                                                              |
78	| Storybook a11y addon                   | `@storybook/addon-a11y`                        | Component-level accessibility checks during development and in Storybook test runs                                                                                                                                  |
79	| Unit test runner                       | Vitest                                         | `vitest.config.ts`; replaces `pwa-kit-dev test` for project tests                                                                                                                                                   |
80	| Accessibility testing                  | axe-core (via `vitest-axe` / `axe-playwright`) | Automated WCAG checks in unit and E2E layers; see Pre-Build Decisions #2 for outstanding items                                                                                                                      |
81	| E2E tests (planned)                    | Playwright                                     | Not yet configured                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
82	| Forms + validation                     | react-hook-form + zod                          | Not yet installed; add when checkout/account work begins                                                                                                                                                            |
83	| Global UI state                        | Zustand                                        | For shared state that outgrows Context (multi-step flows, drawer state, etc.). **SSR note:** initialise store per-request — never as a module singleton — to prevent state leaking across server-rendered requests. |
84	
85	### External services
86	
87	Salesforce Commerce Cloud, Contentful Studio CMS, Global-e (international checkout + server-side pricing/catalogue feed — PRC-34..43 sign-off pending), Didomi (consent), GTM hosted on Addingwell (data layer + downstream tag loading via Tell No Lies). Full integration map below.
88	
89	## Environments
90	
91	Six-tier topology spans **Local → Dev → SIT → UAT → Stage → Prod**. Each tier (other than Local) has its own SFCC realm, Contentful environment, and MuleSoft connections. Ownership splits across three zones — Digital, IT/NewStore, and Shared (Digital + Business).
92	
93	| #   | Tier            | Owner         | Purpose                                                                      | Third-party availability                                              | Deploy trigger                                                              |
94	| --- | --------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
95	| 1   | **Local**       | Digital       | Feature build on developer machines                                          | All services mocked (MSW stubs)                                       | `npm start`                                                                 |
96	| 2   | **Dev**         | Digital       | Integrated digital testing across all 6 storefronts, independent of NewStore | MuleSoft STG · NewStore Dev · Omneo STG · Narvar stub · Adyen sandbox | Merge to `develop`                                                          |
97	| 3   | **SIT**         | IT / NewStore | NewStore SIT and regression on its own cadence                               | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Narvar STG · AP21 test                  | NewStore release cadence (parallel lane, non-blocking for Digital releases) |
98	| 4   | **UAT**         | Shared        | Business acceptance across all 6 regions                                     | NewStore STG · Narvar STG · Omneo STG · Adyen sandbox                 | Business approval gate                                                      |
99	| 5   | **Stage** (E2E) | Shared        | End-to-end testing with all third parties live; time-boxed booked windows    | NewStore STG · MuleSoft STG · Omneo STG · Narvar STG · Adyen sandbox  | Booked 2-week window                                                        |
100	| 6   | **Prod**        | Live          | Production; AU canary then flag-flip to remaining regions                    | NewStore PROD · MuleSoft PROD · Omneo PROD · Narvar PROD · Adyen PROD | Release manager + canary gate                                               |
101	
102	**Stage** is the contractual performance-test environment referenced under [Pre-Build Decisions #3](#3--performance-budgets-) — it mirrors production infrastructure (same MRT bundle class, CDN/edge configuration, SFCC realm tier).
103	
104	**QA workflow** ([`qa.yml`](../.github/workflows/qa.yml)) runs on every PR to `develop` and `release/**`: Vitest unit tests and Storybook interaction + `@storybook/addon-a11y` component-level accessibility checks (`storybook test --ci`), in parallel. Code-correctness checks that run before any environment is involved.
105	
106	**SIT gate** ([`digital-sit.yml`](../.github/workflows/digital-sit.yml)) runs on push/PR to `release/**`: Playwright `p0` specs, bundle-size check, MuleSoft contract tests, Lighthouse CI thresholds, LHCI trend gate. Environment-dependent checks against the deployed Dev tier. On merge to `develop` it also deploys to Dev. Production deploys are gated on a clean SIT gate run plus stakeholder approval through UAT and Stage.
107	
108	**MRT targets** in [mobify.config.js](../mobify.config.js) map one-to-one to the topology: `dev | sit | uat | stage | production`. `ENVIRONMENT_NAME` (`local | dev | sit | uat | stage | prod`) is the per-tier tag emitted to Sentry, New Relic, and GTM.
109	
110	## SSR Requirement (DMU-030)
111	
112	Server-side rendering is **mandatory** for product, category, and content pages (DMU-030, signed off). PWA Kit's SSR pipeline must be preserved — do not introduce client-only patterns (e.g. `typeof window !== 'undefined'` short-circuits, client-only data fetching on first paint, or `next/dynamic`-style `{ ssr: false }`) on these page types. Any componentry that cannot render on the server must be gated behind a hydration-safe boundary that still emits SEO-relevant markup on the server.
113	
114	## Overrides Pattern
115	
116	All customizations live in `overrides/` mirroring the structure of `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/`. Never edit `node_modules/`.
117	
118	**Minimise custom code.** When implementing Zimmermann's design and layout, stay as close to the base PWA Kit implementation as possible. Style changes (CSS, Chakra props, theme tokens) are always expected and need no confirmation. Structural changes — restructuring components, altering data flow, or significantly deviating from base template behaviour — must be confirmed with the user before proceeding.
119	
120	**Before any change:** check whether the file exists in `overrides/`. If not, create the override:
121	
122	1. Copy from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/` to the mirrored path in `overrides/`.
123	2. Rename `.js`/`.jsx` → `.ts`/`.tsx`. Replace `PropTypes` with TypeScript `type` definitions. Add explicit types to all parameters, return values, and props. Use Commerce SDK types (`commerce-sdk-isomorphic`, `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react`) where available. No `as any` or `// @ts-ignore`.
124	3. Verify `npx tsc --noEmit` passes with zero errors.
125	4. **Stop. Present the converted file to the user and wait for approval before making any functional changes.**
126	
127	## New vs. Override Components
128	
129	- **Overriding a base template component:** copy from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/` to the mirrored path in `overrides/` (see Overrides Pattern above).
130	- **Brand-new components** (no base template equivalent): create them in `overrides/app/components/custom/`.
131	
132	## Key Paths
133

160	## Contentful Content Type Management
161	
162	Content types (schema) are never created manually in the Contentful web app. They are defined in code and synced via a script. This makes schema changes reviewable, repeatable, and team-safe.
163	
164	**Key paths:**
165	
166	- `scripts/contentful/sync.js` — runner: upserts (creates or updates) and publishes every content type in the definitions directory
167	- `scripts/contentful/content-types/` — one `.js` file per content type (e.g. `shoppableImage.js`)
168	
169	**To register a new content type:**
170	
171	1. Add a definition file to `scripts/contentful/content-types/<contentTypeId>.js` (see existing files for shape)
172	2. Run `npm run sync:contentful`
173	
174	**To run the sync:**
175	
176	```
177	npm run sync:contentful
178	```
179	
180	Requires `CONTENTFUL_MANAGEMENT_TOKEN` — a personal token tied to your own Contentful account — in `.env.shared` (never commit; run `npm run env -- init` to scaffold it, then `npm run env -- <tier>` to activate a tier before running the sync). Get the token from `app.contentful.com/account/profile/cma_tokens`. `CONTENTFUL_SPACE_ID` is shared across tiers; `CONTENTFUL_ENVIRONMENT_ID` is set per tier and auto-fetched by `npm run env -- init` once the management token is filled in.
181	
182	The script is idempotent — safe to re-run. It preserves any existing fields not in the definition file (it will not delete fields from a live content type).
183	
184	**Relationship to the React component:**
185	Each content type definition in `scripts/contentful/content-types/` corresponds to a React component in `overrides/app/components/contentful/`. The content type's field IDs must match the TypeScript type in `overrides/app/types/contentful.ts`.
186	
187	**Experience Builder components** (drag-and-drop in Contentful Studio) are a separate concern — they are registered in `overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts` and do not need a corresponding `sync:contentful` entry unless they also have a standard content type for use outside Studio.

206	All order-creation, fulfilment write, and CRM sync traffic from SFCC routes through MuleSoft as the middleware layer — SFCC does not call NewStore, AP21, Omneo, or Narvar directly. In addition, the PWA's MRT Node layer calls MuleSoft directly for read operations (order history, order details, boutique / BOPIS stock check, real-time stock availability, GiveX balance check) — SFCC is not in those read paths. A handful of services are also called **browser-direct from the PWA** and another set are **SFCC cartridge integrations** invoked server-side. The `Boundary` column makes this explicit so you know where to look when an integration breaks.

208	**Boundary key:**
209	
210	- **PWA-direct** — called from the browser directly. Vendor key (if any) is publishable/public and safe in the bundle.
211	- **MRT-mediated** — called from the PWA's Node layer via `/mobify/proxy/` or a server-only endpoint. API credentials held as MRT environment variables; never reach the browser bundle. Includes direct PWA → MuleSoft calls via MRT proxy.
212	- **SFCC (OOTB)** — Salesforce-bundled integration; no custom cartridge.
213	- **SFCC (cartridge)** — vendor-supplied or custom server-side cartridge running inside SFCC.
214	- **SFCC → MuleSoft** — SFCC calls MuleSoft, which fans out to the downstream system.
215	- **Browser handoff** — PWA hands the user off to a third party's hosted experience.
216	- **Out-of-band** — no runtime call from PWA or SFCC; the integration delivers data via a separate channel.

249	## Cross-Storefront Session & Basket Scope
250	
251	All eight storefronts are path-prefixed on a single first-party domain and share one SFCC realm with shared customer data. The `httpOnly` SLAS refresh-token cookie set by the SSR layer is therefore presented on every storefront prefix — no cross-domain SSO bridge is needed. SLAS tokens are channel-scoped, so the SSR layer re-initialises the SLAS context per storefront; a registered shopper is silently re-recognised across a storefront switch (shared customer record), while a guest session is site-scoped and does not carry over. **The basket deliberately does not transfer across storefronts** — baskets are site-scoped and priced in the storefront's own currency/pricebook, so a shopper switching storefront starts a fresh basket. Carrying a basket across a currency boundary would produce incorrect pricing. The Global-e checkout handoff is a separate session boundary (Global-e owns its hosted checkout in full). The exact SLAS re-authorisation mechanism and the stay-signed-in UX are open items with the Salesforce integration team.

257	## Blast-Radius Mitigation
258	
259	Multiple upstream integrations (SFCC, MuleSoft/Omneo, Global-e, Narvar, Contentful, Didomi, Inside Chat) mean a failure or attack targeting one service must not cascade. A PWA-relevant mitigation can be done in the SSR layer.
260	
261	The SSR layer in `overrides/app/ssr.js` uses **Node's native `fetch`**, which is backed by `undici`. Undici's `dispatcher` option (the per-call `dispatcher` option on individual `fetch()` invocations) allows each upstream origin to be given its own connection pool with an independent cap. This prevents a slow or flooded integration (e.g. checkout APIs) from exhausting connections for unrelated origins (e.g. Contentful, JWKS).
262	
263	```ts
264	import { Pool } from 'undici';
265	
266	// 1. Create isolated pools for specific origins
267	const checkoutPool = new Pool('https://api.checkout-service.com', {
268	  connections: 10, // Hard limit of 10 concurrent connections to this origin
269	  timeout: 8000,
270	});
271	
272	// 2. Use them explicitly in your fetch calls inside ssr.js
273	async function getCheckoutMetadata() {
274	  return await fetch('https://api.checkout-service.com/v1/metadata', {
275	    dispatcher: checkoutPool, // Safely isolated!
276	  });
277	}
278	```
279	
280	The connection pool split is an engineering decision — the right pool boundaries and sizes depend on observed traffic patterns and the integration map in §7. Planned pools (connection caps should be validated later — see §9.3):
281	
282	| Pool                   | Origin                                                                                                            | Calls                                                                           | Cap | `connectTimeout` | `bodyTimeout` | Reasoning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
283	| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
284	| `sfcc-scapi`           | `https://{shortCode}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com`                                                            | SLAS JWKS (token validation for passwordless login, reset password)             | 5   | 5 s              | 8 s           | `jose` caches the JWK set for its rotation period; actual network calls are rare. GiveX balance calls carry payment credentials in the POST body — a slow MuleSoft response must not hold connections open and starve other pools. Highest cap reflects the broadest call surface. |
