136	**SVG setup**: `<svg width="100%" viewBox="0 0 680 H" role="img"><title>…</title><desc>…</desc>…` — 680px wide, flexible height. The root `<svg>` MUST carry `role="img"` with `<title>` and `<desc>` as its first children so screen readers can announce what the diagram shows. Set H to fit content tightly — the last element's bottom edge + 40px padding. Don't leave excess empty space below the content. Safe area: x=40 to x=640, y=40 to y=(H-40). Background transparent. **Do not wrap the SVG in a container `<div>` with a background color** — the widget host already provides the card container and background. Output the raw `<svg>` element directly.
137	
138	**The 680 in viewBox is load-bearing — do not change it.** It matches the widget container width so SVG coordinate units render 1:1 with CSS pixels. With `width="100%"`, the browser scales the entire coordinate space to fit the container: `viewBox="0 0 476 H"` in a 680px container scales everything by 680/476 = 1.43×, so your `class="th"` 14px text renders at ~20px. The font calibration table below and all "text fits in box" math assume 1:1. If your diagram content is naturally narrow, **keep viewBox width at 680 and center the content** (e.g. content spans x=240..440) — do not shrink the viewBox to hug the content. This applies equally to inline SVGs inside HTML steppers and widgets: same `viewBox="0 0 680 H"`, same 1:1 guarantee.
139	
140	**viewBox height:** After layout, find max_y (bottom-most point of any shape, including text baselines + 4px descent). Set viewBox height = max_y + 20. Don't guess.
141	
142	**text-anchor='end' at x<60 is risky** — the longest label will extend left past x=0. Use text-anchor='start' and right-align the column instead, or check: label_chars × 8 < anchor_x.
143	
144	**One SVG per tool call** — each call must contain exactly one <svg> element. Never leave an abandoned or partial SVG in the output. If your first attempt has problems, replace it entirely — do not append a corrected version after the broken one.
145	
146	**Style rules for all diagrams**:
147	- Every `<text>` element must carry one of the pre-built classes (`t`, `ts`, `th`). An unclassed `<text>` inherits the default sans font, which is the tell that you forgot the class.
148	- Use only two font sizes: 14px for node/region labels (class="t" or "th"), 12px for subtitles, descriptions, and arrow labels (class="ts"). No other sizes.
149	- No decorative step numbers, large numbering, or oversized headings outside boxes.
150	- No icons or illustrations inside boxes — text only. (Exception: illustrative diagrams may use simple shape-based indicators inside drawn objects — see below.)
151	- Sentence case on all labels.
152	
153	**Font size calibration for diagram text labels** - Here's csv table to give you better sense of the Anthropic Sans font rendering width:
154	```csv
155	text, chars length, font-weight, font-size, rendered width
156	Authentication Service, chars: 22, font-weight: 500, font-size: 14px, width: 167px
157	Background Job Processor, chars: 24, font-weight: 500, font-size: 14px, width: 201px
158	Detects and validates incoming tokens, chars: 37, font-weight: 400, font-size: 14px, width: 279px
159	forwards request to, chars: 19, font-weight: 400, font-size: 12px, width: 123px
160	データベースサーバー接続, chars: 12, font-weight: 400, font-size: 14px, width: 181px
161	```
162	
163	Before placing text in a box, check: does (text width + 2×padding) fit the container?
164	
165	**SVG `<text>` never auto-wraps.** Every line break needs an explicit `<tspan x="..." dy="1.2em">`. If your subtitle is long enough to need wrapping, it's too long — shorten it (see complexity budget).
166	
167	**Example check**: You want to put "Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆)" in a rounded rect. The text is 20 characters at 14px ≈ 180px wide. Add 2×24px padding = 228px minimum box width. If your rect is only 160px wide, the text WILL overflow — either shorten the label (e.g. just "Glucose") or widen the box. Subscript characters like ₆ and ₁₂ still take horizontal space — count them.
168	
169	**Pre-built classes** (already loaded in SVG widget):
170	- `class="t"` = sans 14px primary, `class="ts"` = sans 12px secondary, `class="th"` = sans 14px medium (500)
171	- `class="box"` = neutral rect (`--surface-1` fill, `--border-strong` stroke)
172	- `class="node"` = clickable group with hover effect (cursor pointer, slight dim on hover)
173	- `class="arr"` = arrow line (1.5px, open chevron head)
174	- `class="leader"` = dashed leader line (tertiary stroke, 0.5px, dashed)
175	- `class="c-{ramp}"` = colored node (c-blue, c-teal, c-amber, c-green, c-red, c-purple, c-coral, c-pink, c-gray). Apply to `<g>` or shape element (rect/circle/ellipse), NOT to paths. Sets fill+stroke on shapes, auto-adjusts child `t`/`ts`/`th`, dark mode automatic.
176	
177	**c-{ramp} nesting:** These classes use direct-child selectors (`>`). Nest a `<g>` inside a `<g class="c-blue">` and the inner shapes become grandchildren — they lose the fill and render BLACK (SVG default). Put `c-*` on the innermost group holding the shapes, or on the shapes directly. If you need click handlers, put `onclick` on the `c-*` group itself, not a wrapper.
178	
179	- Short aliases: `var(--p)`, `var(--s)`, `var(--t)`, `var(--bg2)`, `var(--b)`
180	- Arrow marker: always include this `<defs>` at the start of every SVG:
181	  `<defs><marker id="arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M2 1L8 5L2 9" fill="none" stroke="context-stroke" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/></marker></defs>`
182	  Then use `marker-end="url(#arrow)"` on lines. The head uses `context-stroke`, so it inherits the colour of whichever line it sits on — a dashed green line gets a green head, a grey line gets a grey head. Never a colour mismatch. Do not add filters or extra markers to `<defs>`. `<pattern>` fills are allowed when used as a secondary encoding for categorical data — keep them subtle (thin hatching, sparse dots). Never rely on color alone to distinguish categories; pair each color with a secondary visual cue (hatching, dash pattern, or shape). Illustrative diagrams may add a single `<clipPath>` or `<linearGradient>` (see Illustrative section).
183	
184	**Minimize standalone labels.** Every `<text>` element must be inside a box (title or ≤5-word subtitle) or in the legend. Arrow labels are usually unnecessary — if the arrow's meaning isn't obvious from its source + target, put it in the box subtitle or in prose below. Labels floating in space collide with things and are ambiguous.
185	
186	**Stroke width:** Use 0.5px strokes for diagram borders and edges — not 1px or 2px. Thin strokes feel more refined.
187	
188	**Connector paths need `fill="none"`.** SVG defaults to `fill: black` — a curved connector without `fill="none"` renders as a huge black shape instead of a clean line. Every `<path>` or `<polyline>` used as a connector/arrow MUST have `fill="none"`. Only set fill on shapes meant to be filled (rects, circles, polygons).
189	
190	**Rect rounding:** `rx="4"` for subtle corners. `rx="8"` max for emphasized rounding. `rx` ≥ half the height = pill shape — deliberate only.
191	
192	**Schematic containers use dashed rects with a label.** Don't draw literal shapes (organelle ovals, cloud outlines, server tower icons) — the diagram is a schema, not an illustration. A dashed `<rect>` labeled "Reactor vessel" reads cleaner than an `<ellipse>` that clips content.
193	
194	**Lines stop at component edges.** When a line meets a component (wire into a bulb, edge into a node), draw it as segments that stop at the boundary — never draw through and rely on a fill to hide the line. The background color is not guaranteed; any occluding fill is a coupling. Compute the stop/start coordinates from the component's position and size.
195	
196	**Physical-color scenes (sky, water, grass, skin, materials):** Use ALL hardcoded hex — never mix with `c-*` theme classes. The scene should not invert in dark mode. If you need a dark variant, provide it explicitly with `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — this is the one place that's allowed. Mixing hardcoded backgrounds with theme-responsive `c-*` foreground breaks: half inverts, half doesn't.
197	
198	**No rotated text**. `<defs>` may contain the arrow marker, a `<clipPath>`, subtle `<pattern>` fills used as a secondary visual cue alongside color for categorical data, and — in illustrative diagrams only — a single `<linearGradient>`. Nothing else: no filters, no extra markers.
199	
200	
201	## Diagram types
202	*"Explain how compound interest works" / "How does a process scheduler work"*
203	
204	**Two rules that cause most diagram failures — check these before writing each arrow and each box:**
205	1. **Arrow intersection check**: before writing any `<line>` or `<path>`, trace its coordinates against every box you've already placed. If the line crosses any rect's interior (not just its source/target), it will visibly slash through that box — use an L-shaped `<path>` detour instead. This applies to arrows crossing labels too.
206	2. **Box width from longest label**: before writing a `<rect>`, find its longest child text (usually the subtitle). `rect_width = max(title_chars × 8, subtitle_chars × 7) + 24`. A 100px-wide box holds at most a 10-char subtitle. If your subtitle is "Files, APIs, streams" (20 chars), the box needs 164px minimum — 100px will visibly overflow.
207	
208	**Tier packing:** Compute total width BEFORE placing. Example — 4 pub/sub consumer boxes:
209	- WRONG: x=40,160,260,360 w=160 → 40-60px overlaps (4×160=640 > 480 available)
210	- RIGHT: x=50,200,350,500 w=130 gap=20 → fits (4×130 + 3×20 = 580 ≤ 590 safe width; right edge at 630 ≤ 640)
211	Work bottom-up for trees: size leaf tier first, parent width ≥ sum of children.
212	
213	**Diagrams are the hardest use case** — they have the highest failure rate due to precise coordinate math. Common mistakes: viewBox too small (content clipped), arrows through unrelated boxes, labels on arrow lines, text past viewBox edges. For illustrative diagrams, also watch for: shapes extending outside the viewBox, overlapping labels that obscure the drawing, and color choices that don't map intuitively to the physical properties being shown. Double-check coordinates before finalizing.
214	
215	Use SVG for diagrams. The widget automatically wraps SVG output in a card.
216	
217	**Pick the right diagram type.** The decision is about *intent*, not subject matter. Ask: is the user trying to *document* this, or *understand* it?
218	
219	**Reference diagrams** — the user wants a map they can point at. Precision matters more than feeling. Boxes, labels, arrows, containment. These are the diagrams you'd find in documentation.
220	- **Flowchart** — steps in sequence, decisions branching, data transforming. Good for: approval workflows, request lifecycles, build pipelines, "what happens when I click submit". Trigger phrases: *"walk me through the process"*, *"what are the steps"*, *"what's the flow"*.
221	- **Structural diagram** — things inside other things. Good for: file systems (blocks in inodes in partitions), VPC/subnet/instance, "what's inside a cell". Trigger phrases: *"what's the architecture"*, *"how is this organised"*, *"where does X live"*.
222	
223	**Intuition diagrams** — the user wants to *feel* how something works. The goal isn't a correct map, it's the right mental model. These should look nothing like a flowchart. The subject doesn't need a physical form — it needs a *visual metaphor*.
224	- **Illustrative diagram** — draw the mechanism. Physical things get cross-sections (water heaters, engines, lungs). Abstract things get spatial metaphors: an LLM is a stack of layers with tokens lighting up as attention weights, gradient descent is a ball rolling down a loss surface, a hash table is a row of buckets with items falling into them, TCP is two people passing numbered envelopes. Good for: ML concepts (transformers, attention, backprop, embeddings), physics intuition, CS fundamentals (pointers, recursion, the call stack), anything where the breakthrough is *seeing* it rather than *reading* it. Trigger phrases: *"how does X actually work"*, *"explain X"*, *"I don't get X"*, *"give me an intuition for X"*.
225	
226	**Route on the verb, not the noun.** Same subject, different diagram depending on what was asked:
227	
228	| User says | Type | What to draw |
229	|---|---|---|
230	| "how do LLMs work" | **Illustrative** | Token row, stacked layer slabs, attention threads glowing warm between tokens. Go interactive if you can. |
231	| "transformer architecture" | Structural | Labelled boxes: embedding, attention heads, FFN, layer norm. |
232	| "how does attention work" | **Illustrative** | One query token, a fan of lines to every key, line opacity = weight. |
233	| "how does gradient descent work" | **Illustrative** | Contour surface, a ball, a trail of steps. Slider for learning rate. |
234	| "what are the training steps" | Flowchart | Forward → loss → backward → update. Boxes and arrows. |
235	| "how does TCP work" | **Illustrative** | Two endpoints, numbered packets in flight, an ACK returning. |
236	| "TCP handshake sequence" | Flowchart | SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. Three boxes. |
237	| "explain the Krebs cycle" / "how does the event loop work" | **HTML stepper** | Click through stages. Never a ring. |
238	| "how does a hash map work" | **Illustrative** | Key falling through a funnel into one of N buckets. |
239	| "draw the database schema" / "show me the ERD" | **mermaid.js** | `erDiagram` syntax. Not SVG. |
240	
241	The illustrative route is the default for *"how does X work"* with no further qualification. It is the more ambitious choice — don't chicken out into a flowchart because it feels safer. Claude draws these well.
242	
243	Don't mix families in one diagram. If you need both, draw the intuition version first (build the mental model), then the reference version (fill in the precise labels) as a second tool call with prose between.
244	
245	**For complex topics, use multiple SVG calls** — break the explanation into a series of smaller diagrams rather than one dense diagram. Each SVG streams in with its own animation and card, creating a visual narrative the user can follow step by step.
246	
247	**Always add prose between diagrams** — never stack multiple SVG calls back-to-back without text. Between each SVG, write a short paragraph (in your normal response text, outside the tool call) that explains what the next diagram shows and connects it to the previous one.

content.text:
Now let's walk through it properly.

## 1. SFCC vs. PWA Kit — the ELI5 version

Think of it like a restaurant:

- **Salesforce Commerce Cloud (SFCC)** is the **kitchen and the pantry** — it holds the actual product catalogue, prices, carts, orders, and customer accounts. It's the "system of record" for commerce.
- **PWA Kit** is the **dining room and the waiter** — it's the actual website your customer sees and clicks around in (built in React). It doesn't store commerce data itself; it asks SFCC for it through an API (`@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react`) and renders it as a fast, pretty, SEO-friendly page.
- **Managed Runtime (MRT)** is **where the waiter's podium sits** — it's Salesforce's hosting platform that runs the PWA's Node.js server (server-side rendering, proxying calls, holding secrets). "PWA Kit" is the framework/code; "MRT" is where that code actually runs once deployed.

The first diagram shows this: the customer's browser talks to **PWA Kit (MRT)**, and MRT is the one hub that fans out to everything else — it never talks to backend systems like NewStore or Omneo directly. Four kinds of "everything else":

- **SFCC** — products, cart, orders, domestic checkout.
- **Contentful** — the CMS for editorial content (homepage banners, size guides, promo content) — a completely separate system from SFCC, browser-direct.
- **MuleSoft** — the "phone operator" middleware. SFCC never calls NewStore (order management), AP21 (loyalty/product master), Omneo (CRM), or Narvar (delivery/tracking) directly — it always goes through MuleSoft. The PWA's server layer also calls MuleSoft *directly* for a handful of read-only things (order history, stock checks, gift-card balance) without going through SFCC at all.
- **Third-party, browser-direct** — things like Adyen's payment widget, Didomi (cookie consent), and GTM (tag manager) that load straight in the browser once the customer has given consent. Full list and rationale per system: [.docs/integration/](.docs/integration/) (one file per vendor) and [architecture.md §Integration Map](.docs/architecture.md:204).

**Key rule that trips people up:** all 8 storefronts (AU, UK, US domestic/international, 4× EU, HK, ME) run on **one PWA Kit codebase** and **one SFCC realm**, sharing customer identity, but each has its **own basket, currency, and pricebook** — a basket never carries over between storefronts, by design (switching currency mid-basket would mis-price it).

## 2. Environments — where code actually lands

Six tiers, and this is where I hit a **live documentation conflict** worth knowing about as FED Lead: [architecture.md](.docs/architecture.md:91) (in-repo) orders them Local→Dev→SIT→**UAT→Stage**→Prod, but Confluence's [Environment Topology & Promotion Path](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/304840708) — the page with the actual entry-criteria logic — orders them Local→Dev→SIT→**Stage→UAT**→Prod. I've gone with Confluence's order below (it has the real gating rules), and logged this as a fresh conflict in project memory, but it's worth raising with the Integration lead since [projectState.md](.docs/memory/projectState.md) claims this was already "reconciled across docs" on 2026-07-16 and evidently wasn't, at least not in architecture.md.

The second diagram shows the pipeline. A confusing naming collision to internalise early: **"SIT" means two different things** here —

1. **"Digital SIT Gate"** — an automated CI check (Playwright, Lighthouse, bundle-size, MuleSoft contract tests) that runs on every PR and gates promotion into **Dev**.
2. **The "SIT" tier/environment** — a separate MRT environment where NewStore's team runs their own 2–3 month order-management test cycle, in parallel, on its own schedule. It never blocks the Digital pipeline (that's what "non-blocking" means in the diagram).

The two only meet at **Stage**: Stage won't open until *both* the Digital SIT Gate is green on a `release/*` branch *and* NewStore signs off that their SIT cycle is complete. From there, UAT is business sign-off across all 6 regions, then Prod deploys AU first as a canary (error rate must stay under 0.5% for 2 hours before the rest of the world gets flipped on).

Each tier also has its **own dedicated SFCC sandbox, Contentful environment, and MuleSoft connection** — nothing is shared, so a bug in Dev's SFCC data can't leak into SIT's.

## 3. Where the project actually stands right now (reality check)

The six-tier pipeline above is the **designed target**, not yet the lived reality. As of my last check (2026-08-03), **no `release/*` branch has ever been created** in this repo — only `develop`, `main`, and feature branches exist. Concretely:

- Everything that's happened so far is **Local → Dev** (`npm start` locally, merge to `develop` auto-deploys to Dev).
- Stage, UAT, and Prod are configured in principle (`mobify.config.js` targets, environment-switching tooling) but haven't been exercised yet — release-branch protection, SIT secrets, and the SIT MRT environment are still being stood up (tracked on Confluence's [7.1c CI/CD & Environment Setup Checklist](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/305430530)).
- This isn't a red flag — it's tracked and expected: the epic that owns this setup (Jira `SFCC-1`, "Platform Setup & Environments") is still open, and the current sprint (`SFCC-254`) is actively standing up Dev/Test/SIT/UAT environments for all 8 storefronts right now.
- There's also an **unimplemented proposal** on Confluence to switch from branch-based to **tag-based** promotion (`v0.1.0-rc.1` style tags instead of moving branch refs) for everything past Dev — worth knowing about since it may change how "promotion" works before you see a real release.

## 4. Where the pieces genuinely stand today (per `projectState.md`)

Almost every third-party integration is still pointed at **mock/sandbox accounts**, not production — SFCC, Contentful, Global-e, Didomi, Omneo, MuleSoft, Adyen, GiveX, etc. are all "Not started" for production wiring. What's actually built: PWA Kit scaffolding, the overrides pattern, country/locale config, the Contentful content-type sync, a first-pass header, and the environment-switching tooling (`npm run env`). The project is in **Detailed Design** phase — most functional requirements are signed off, but no production build has started beyond scaffolding.

## Where to go deeper

| Topic | Doc |
|---|---|
| Full integration map (all ~25 systems, boundary classes, credentials) | [architecture.md §Integration Map](.docs/architecture.md:204), [.docs/integration/*.md](.docs/integration/index.md) (one file per vendor) |
| Canonical architecture TSD | Confluence 256835585 "Technical Solution Design – PWA" |
| Environment credentials/URLs per tier | Confluence 285540356 "05.6 Environment Details" |
| Branching rules | [AGENTS.md § Branch Rules](AGENTS.md), Confluence 304840733 "Branching Guide (GitFlow)" |
| CI/CD pipeline detail | Confluence 305561601 / 304840754, [.github/workflows/](.github/workflows/) |
| Live project status | [.docs/memory/projectState.md](.docs/memory/projectState.md) |

Given how much is still "designed but not yet exercised," my honest suggestion as you ramp up: treat the six-tier pipeline as the map, not the territory — ask the Integration lead directly whether Stage/UAT ordering and the tag-based promotion proposal have actually been decided, since those are exactly the kind of thing that's easy to plan around wrong if you take either doc at face value.

1	# 01 — Salesforce Commerce Cloud (SCAPI) + reCAPTCHA
2	
3	## 1. Purpose and scope
4	
5	Salesforce Commerce Cloud B2C (SFCC) is the system of record for commerce data. The storefront calls SFCC directly from the browser via SCAPI for browsing, basket management, customer accounts, and order placement.
6	
7	In scope:
8	
9	- Authentication via Shopper Login & API Access Service (SLAS)
10	- Product catalogue, categories, search, recommendations
11	- Basket and cart
12	- Customer account (authentication record) and saved-payment token references
13	- Order placement for SFCC-owned checkouts (domestic markets)
14	- Gift cards — the storefront applies them via SCAPI; server-side redemption is outside the PWA boundary
15	- Google reCAPTCHA — browser-side script load on register/login forms; MRT-side token verification before SCAPI submission
16	
17	At migration, only the customer's email and Omneo ID are stored in SFCC. Name, phone, addresses, and communication preferences come from Omneo at login (DMU-004). Order history comes from MuleSoft via the MRT proxy, not from SFCC (DMU-007).
18	
19	Out of scope of this document:
20	
21	- GiveX validate/redeem/refund, Avalara tax, Adyen back-office — all server-side, outside the PWA
22	- SFCC ↔ MuleSoft flows to NewStore, AP21, Omneo, Narvar
23	- Booxi appointment booking — MRT-mediated (PWA → MRT → Booxi), not a SFCC flow
24	- Business Manager configuration: promotions rules, content slots, Page Designer pages
25	
26	## 2. Browser-side architecture
27	
28	```
29	PWA (React, SSR + CSR)
30	        │
31	        │  @salesforce/commerce-sdk-react (TanStack Query under the hood)
32	        ▼
33	SLAS auth (guest or registered shopper) ──► Shopper context
34	        │                                       (site, currency, locale, customer)
35	        ▼
36	SCAPI: products, search, baskets, orders, customers, promotions, gift cards
37	        │
38	        ▼
39	SFCC realm
40	```
41	
42	- **Single SDK.** `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react` handles every SFCC call — SLAS token lifecycle, retry, and TanStack Query caching.
43	- **SSR and CSR.** Catalogue, PDP, PLP, content, and boutique pages are server-rendered for SEO and LCP. Cart, checkout, My Account, and order pages render an SSR shell and hydrate personalised data client-side after auth.
44	- **Managed Runtime.** The PWA Kit Node layer hosts the SSR pipeline and routes SLAS private-client calls through the server-side proxy.
45	
46	## 3. Authentication and credentials
47	
48	- **SLAS private-client flow** issues two token types: a guest access token (anonymous shopper, refreshed silently) and a registered shopper access token (issued after email/password login). Tokens are JWTs with a customer ID, unique shopper ID (USID), and refresh token.
49	- **Refresh tokens live in `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookies** set by the SSR layer. Browser JavaScript never sees the raw refresh token. On each refresh SLAS regenerates the token and voids the old one; the SSR layer rewrites the cookie in the same response.
50	- **Private client credentials.** The SLAS client secret is an MRT environment variable and never reaches the browser. The authorisation code exchange goes through the MRT private-client proxy (`privateClientProxyEndpoint`). The SLAS client ID and SCAPI short code stay in the bundle as public identifiers.
51	- **Social login.** Apple and Google via SLAS third-party identity-provider federation — confirmed in scope for launch; implementation design still open.
52	- **No Open Commerce API (OCAPI) credentials in the browser.** Any operation not yet covered by SCAPI is proxied through Managed Runtime with OCAPI credentials held server-side.
53	
54	### Magento password migration (CFD-013)
55	
56	Passwords were not migrated from Magento. All existing customers must reset at go-live. Failed sign-ins return a generic "invalid credentials" message (no email-existence leak) and the "forgot password" link is always visible.
57	
58	### Cross-storefront session continuity
59	
60	All eight storefronts are path-prefixed on a single domain and share one SFCC realm.
61	
62	- **The refresh-token cookie is shared across storefronts.** Every storefront lives on the same domain, so the `httpOnly` cookie is sent on every path prefix. No cross-domain SSO bridge is needed.
63	- **Tokens are channel-scoped.** A token issued for `zimm-au` is not valid for `zimm-uk` — this is a hard SLAS platform constraint. On a storefront switch the SSR layer performs a fresh authorisation for the destination channel using the SLAS Trusted System on Behalf (TSOB) flow: it calls `getTrustedSystemAccessToken` with the shopper's `login_id`, which issues a new channel-scoped token server-side without prompting the customer. A registered shopper stays signed in transparently. A guest session does not carry over — guest tokens and baskets are site-scoped. **TSOB rate limit:** SLAS returns HTTP 409 if multiple TSOB calls are made for the same shopper within a 3-second window — the SSR layer must not fire duplicate TSOB calls on rapid storefront switches (debounce or dedupe at the MRT layer).
64	- **Baskets do not transfer — by design.** Baskets are site-scoped and priced in the storefront's own currency. Switching storefront starts a fresh basket; carrying one across a currency boundary would produce wrong prices.
65	- **Checkout handoff is a separate boundary.** When handing off to Global-e, the SLAS session does not extend into Global-e's hosted checkout.
66	
67	## 4. Data exchanged
68	
69	| Resource                           | Verbs                    | Notes                                                                                                                                           |
70	| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
71	| `/checkout/shopper-login/oauth2/*` | GET, POST                | SLAS authentication and token lifecycle                                                                                                         |
72	| `/product/shopper-products/v1/*`   | GET                      | Product details, master/variant resolution                                                                                                      |
73	| `/search/shopper-search/v1/*`      | GET                      | Catalogue search, faceting, sort, suggestions                                                                                                   |
74	| `/checkout/shopper-baskets/v2/*`   | GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE | Basket lifecycle, line items, shipments, payment instruments                                                                                    |
75	| `/checkout/shopper-orders/v1/*`    | POST, GET                | Order placement and lookup (SFCC-owned checkouts only)                                                                                          |
76	| `/customer/shopper-customers/v1/*` | GET, POST, PATCH         | Profile, addresses, saved-payment references                                                                                                    |
77	| `/pricing/shopper-promotions/v1/*` | GET                      | Active promotions, coupon validation                                                                                                            |
78	| Einstein recommendations endpoints | GET                      | Personalised recommendations slot. Consent-gated (Didomi purpose TBC) — falls back to a static SFCC merchandising group if consent is not given |
79	
80	Every request carries the site ID, organisation ID, locale, currency, and SLAS bearer token. PII travels over TLS only. PCI scope is Adyen's — SFCC holds token references only.
81	
82	## 5. reCAPTCHA on register and login (CRM-008)
83	
84	- The storefront loads the reCAPTCHA v3 script on register and login forms only — not on any other page — and only after the customer first touches the form, so the script never blocks first paint.
85	- On submit, the reCAPTCHA token is sent alongside the form data to the MRT layer. The MRT layer verifies the token against Google's `siteverify` endpoint (using the secret key held as the `RECAPTCHA_SECRET_KEY` MRT environment variable) before forwarding the request to SCAPI. The secret key never reaches the browser.
86	- The site key is set per environment as `RECAPTCHA_SITE_KEY` (MRT environment variable, public). The secret key is held as `RECAPTCHA_SECRET_KEY` (MRT environment variable, server-only).
87	- reCAPTCHA loads on form interaction regardless of consent. **Exception: EU and UK** — in those regions it only loads after Didomi consent, which means a visitor who declines gets no bot protection there.
88	
89	## 6. Performance and loading strategy
90	
91	- **HTTP/2** to a single SCAPI host; `<link rel="preconnect">` emitted in the document head.
92	- **TanStack Query** dedupes in-flight requests. Working defaults: stale time 60 s for catalogue, 30 s for promotions, 0 s for basket (always fresh).
93	- **SFCC edge cache** for anonymous catalogue traffic; cache keys include site, locale, currency, and customer group.
94	- **Parallel calls on PDP.** Product, recommendations, and promotions are fetched in parallel — no waterfall.
95	- **SSR fetches only critical data.** Recommendations and reviews load client-side after hydration.
96	- **Field projection.** SCAPI `fields=` parameters are used where supported to reduce payload size.
97	
98	## 7. Multi-region behaviour
99	
100	SFCC site IDs and Business Manager locale IDs verified against bkzk-002 Business Manager (2026-06-13):
101	
102	| SFCC Site ID               | BM Locale ID                                  | URL prefix                                 | Currency               | Checkout owner              |
103	| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- | --------------------------- |
104	| `ZimmermannAU`             | `en`                                          | `/` (root, x-default hreflang)             | AUD                    | SFCC                        |
105	| `ZimmermannUS`             | `en-US`                                       | `/us/`                                     | USD                    | SFCC (US domestic)          |
106	| `ZimmermannUSIntl` _(TBC)_ | `en-US` _(TBC)_                               | `/en-ca/`                                  | USD                    | Global-e (US international) |
107	| `ZimmermannUK`             | `en-GB`                                       | `/uk/`                                     | GBP                    | SFCC                        |
108	| `ZimmermannEU`             | `en-GB` (EN), `fr` (FR), `it` (IT), `es` (ES) | `/en-eu/`, `/fr-eu/`, `/it-eu/`, `/es-eu/` | EUR                    | SFCC                        |
109	| `ZimmermannEUIntl`         | `en-CH`                                       | `/en-ch/`                                  | EUR                    | Global-e                    |
110	| `ZimmermannHK`             | `en-HK`                                       | `/hk/`                                     | HKD (SFCC price books) | Global-e                    |
111	| `ZimmermannME`             | `en-AE`                                       | `/en-ae/`                                  | AED (SFCC price books) | Global-e                    |
112	
113	- The site ID is resolved from the URL prefix on every request (SSR and CSR).
114	- AU is geo-redirected for non-Oceania human visitors; verified search bots and social unfurlers are exempt via UA allowlist.
115	- Per-environment SLAS client ID and SCAPI short code remain outstanding — see §11 item 2.
116	
117	## 8. Failure modes and graceful degradation
118	
119	| Failure                                       | Behaviour                                                                                                                                                                       |
120	| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
121	| SLAS unavailable                              | Storefront cannot mint a guest token and is non-operational. Show a maintenance message. P1 incident.                                                                           |
122	| SCAPI catalogue 5xx                           | TanStack Query retries three times with exponential backoff. On final failure, show the last cached payload if available; otherwise show an error state with a "Try again" CTA. |
123	| SCAPI basket 5xx during add-to-cart           | Inline error toast. The user's intent stays in client state so a retry resends the same request.                                                                                |
124	| Order placement 5xx after Adyen authorisation | Hard error — the order cannot fail silently. The customer sees an explicit error with a contact reference and ops is alerted.                                                   |
125	| Einstein recommendations 5xx                  | Hide the slot or fall back to a static merchandising group.                                                                                                                     |
126	| SLAS token refresh fails                      | Force re-login. The basket is preserved on the guest token until the customer completes checkout.                                                                               |
127	| TSOB 409 (rapid storefront switch)            | Retry after 3 seconds. Do not re-login the customer — the existing session is still valid on the origin channel.                                                                |
128	| reCAPTCHA fails to load or token rejected     | Block the register/login submit, show a "please retry" message, and offer a contact-support path after two failures.                                                            |
129	
130	## 9. Security and privacy
131	
132	- All traffic is TLS 1.2+ over HTTPS.
133	- SLAS private-client flow — the authorisation code exchange is proxied through MRT so the client secret never reaches the browser.
134	- Refresh tokens are held in `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookies — never in browser JavaScript.
135	- PCI scope is Adyen's — the browser sends payment data directly to Adyen. SFCC holds token references only.
136	
137	## 10. Open items requiring client confirmation
138	
139	1. **Login MFA scope.** Confirm whether multi-factor authentication on login is in scope for launch or post-launch. If in scope, the SLAS configuration and the PWA login flow need additional design.
140	
141	2. **`sfPayments.metadataUrl` hostname.** The `sfcc-payments` undici connection pool (TSD §12.1) holds `config.app.sfPayments.metadataUrl`'s origin in a pool separate from `sfcc-scapi` (`{shortCode}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com`). That separation only provides blast-radius isolation if the two hosts are different origins. If `sfPayments.metadataUrl` resolves to the same SCAPI host, the pools should be merged.

# 01 — Salesforce Commerce Cloud (SCAPI) + reCAPTCHA

## 1. Purpose and scope

Salesforce Commerce Cloud B2C (SFCC) is the system of record for commerce data. The storefront calls SFCC directly from the browser via SCAPI for browsing, basket management, customer accounts, and order placement.

In scope:

- Authentication via Shopper Login & API Access Service (SLAS)
- Product catalogue, categories, search, recommendations
- Basket and cart
- Customer account (authentication record) and saved-payment token references
- Order placement for SFCC-owned checkouts (domestic markets)
- Gift cards — the storefront applies them via SCAPI; server-side redemption is outside the PWA boundary
- Google reCAPTCHA — browser-side script load on register/login forms; MRT-side token verification before SCAPI submission

At migration, only the customer's email and Omneo ID are stored in SFCC. Name, phone, addresses, and communication preferences come from Omneo at login (DMU-004). Order history comes from MuleSoft via the MRT proxy, not from SFCC (DMU-007).

Out of scope of this document:

- GiveX validate/redeem/refund, Avalara tax, Adyen back-office — all server-side, outside the PWA
- SFCC ↔ MuleSoft flows to NewStore, AP21, Omneo, Narvar
- Booxi appointment booking — MRT-mediated (PWA → MRT → Booxi), not a SFCC flow
- Business Manager configuration: promotions rules, content slots, Page Designer pages

## 2. Browser-side architecture

```
PWA (React, SSR + CSR)
        │
        │  @salesforce/commerce-sdk-react (TanStack Query under the hood)
        ▼
SLAS auth (guest or registered shopper) ──► Shopper context
        │                                       (site, currency, locale, customer)
        ▼
SCAPI: products, search, baskets, orders, customers, promotions, gift cards
        │
        ▼
SFCC realm
```

- **Single SDK.** `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react` handles every SFCC call — SLAS token lifecycle, retry, and TanStack Query caching.
- **SSR and CSR.** Catalogue, PDP, PLP, content, and boutique pages are server-rendered for SEO and LCP. Cart, checkout, My Account, and order pages render an SSR shell and hydrate personalised data client-side after auth.
- **Managed Runtime.** The PWA Kit Node layer hosts the SSR pipeline and routes SLAS private-client calls through the server-side proxy.

## 3. Authentication and credentials

- **SLAS private-client flow** issues two token types: a guest access token (anonymous shopper, refreshed silently) and a registered shopper access token (issued after email/password login). Tokens are JWTs with a customer ID, unique shopper ID (USID), and refresh token.
- **Refresh tokens live in `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookies** set by the SSR layer. Browser JavaScript never sees the raw refresh token. On each refresh SLAS regenerates the token and voids the old one; the SSR layer rewrites the cookie in the same response.
- **Private client credentials.** The SLAS client secret is an MRT environment variable and never reaches the browser. The authorisation code exchange goes through the MRT private-client proxy (`privateClientProxyEndpoint`). The SLAS client ID and SCAPI short code stay in the bundle as public identifiers.
- **Social login.** Apple and Google via SLAS third-party identity-provider federation — confirmed in scope for launch; implementation design still open.
- **No Open Commerce API (OCAPI) credentials in the browser.** Any operation not yet covered by SCAPI is proxied through Managed Runtime with OCAPI credentials held server-side.

### Magento password migration (CFD-013)

Passwords were not migrated from Magento. All existing customers must reset at go-live. Failed sign-ins return a generic "invalid credentials" message (no email-existence leak) and the "forgot password" link is always visible.

### Cross-storefront session continuity

All eight storefronts are path-prefixed on a single domain and share one SFCC realm.

- **The refresh-token cookie is shared across storefronts.** Every storefront lives on the same domain, so the `httpOnly` cookie is sent on every path prefix. No cross-domain SSO bridge is needed.
- **Tokens are channel-scoped.** A token issued for `zimm-au` is not valid for `zimm-uk` — this is a hard SLAS platform constraint. On a storefront switch the SSR layer performs a fresh authorisation for the destination channel using the SLAS Trusted System on Behalf (TSOB) flow: it calls `getTrustedSystemAccessToken` with the shopper's `login_id`, which issues a new channel-scoped token server-side without prompting the customer. A registered shopper stays signed in transparently. A guest session does not carry over — guest tokens and baskets are site-scoped. **TSOB rate limit:** SLAS returns HTTP 409 if multiple TSOB calls are made for the same shopper within a 3-second window — the SSR layer must not fire duplicate TSOB calls on rapid storefront switches (debounce or dedupe at the MRT layer).
- **Baskets do not transfer — by design.** Baskets are site-scoped and priced in the storefront's own currency. Switching storefront starts a fresh basket; carrying one across a currency boundary would produce wrong prices.
- **Checkout handoff is a separate boundary.** When handing off to Global-e, the SLAS session does not extend into Global-e's hosted checkout.

## 4. Data exchanged

| Resource                           | Verbs                    | Notes                                                                                                                                           |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/checkout/shopper-login/oauth2/*` | GET, POST                | SLAS authentication and token lifecycle                                                                                                         |
| `/product/shopper-products/v1/*`   | GET                      | Product details, master/variant resolution                                                                                                      |
| `/search/shopper-search/v1/*`      | GET                      | Catalogue search, faceting, sort, suggestions                                                                                                   |
| `/checkout/shopper-baskets/v2/*`   | GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE | Basket lifecycle, line items, shipments, payment instruments                                                                                    |
| `/checkout/shopper-orders/v1/*`    | POST, GET                | Order placement and lookup (SFCC-owned checkouts only)                                                                                          |
| `/customer/shopper-customers/v1/*` | GET, POST, PATCH         | Profile, addresses, saved-payment references                                                                                                    |
| `/pricing/shopper-promotions/v1/*` | GET                      | Active promotions, coupon validation                                                                                                            |
| Einstein recommendations endpoints | GET                      | Personalised recommendations slot. Consent-gated (Didomi purpose TBC) — falls back to a static SFCC merchandising group if consent is not given |

Every request carries the site ID, organisation ID, locale, currency, and SLAS bearer token. PII travels over TLS only. PCI scope is Adyen's — SFCC holds token references only.

## 5. reCAPTCHA on register and login (CRM-008)

- The storefront loads the reCAPTCHA v3 script on register and login forms only — not on any other page — and only after the customer first touches the form, so the script never blocks first paint.
- On submit, the reCAPTCHA token is sent alongside the form data to the MRT layer. The MRT layer verifies the token against Google's `siteverify` endpoint (using the secret key held as the `RECAPTCHA_SECRET_KEY` MRT environment variable) before forwarding the request to SCAPI. The secret key never reaches the browser.
- The site key is set per environment as `RECAPTCHA_SITE_KEY` (MRT environment variable, public). The secret key is held as `RECAPTCHA_SECRET_KEY` (MRT environment variable, server-only).
- reCAPTCHA loads on form interaction regardless of consent. **Exception: EU and UK** — in those regions it only loads after Didomi consent, which means a visitor who declines gets no bot protection there.

## 6. Performance and loading strategy

- **HTTP/2** to a single SCAPI host; `<link rel="preconnect">` emitted in the document head.
- **TanStack Query** dedupes in-flight requests. Working defaults: stale time 60 s for catalogue, 30 s for promotions, 0 s for basket (always fresh).
- **SFCC edge cache** for anonymous catalogue traffic; cache keys include site, locale, currency, and customer group.
- **Parallel calls on PDP.** Product, recommendations, and promotions are fetched in parallel — no waterfall.
- **SSR fetches only critical data.** Recommendations and reviews load client-side after hydration.
- **Field projection.** SCAPI `fields=` parameters are used where supported to reduce payload size.

## 7. Multi-region behaviour

SFCC site IDs and Business Manager locale IDs verified against bkzk-002 Business Manager (2026-06-13):

| SFCC Site ID               | BM Locale ID                                  | URL prefix                                 | Currency               | Checkout owner              |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `ZimmermannAU`             | `en`                                          | `/` (root, x-default hreflang)             | AUD                    | SFCC                        |
| `ZimmermannUS`             | `en-US`                                       | `/us/`                                     | USD                    | SFCC (US domestic)          |
| `ZimmermannUSIntl` _(TBC)_ | `en-US` _(TBC)_                               | `/en-ca/`                                  | USD                    | Global-e (US international) |
| `ZimmermannUK`             | `en-GB`                                       | `/uk/`                                     | GBP                    | SFCC                        |
| `ZimmermannEU`             | `en-GB` (EN), `fr` (FR), `it` (IT), `es` (ES) | `/en-eu/`, `/fr-eu/`, `/it-eu/`, `/es-eu/` | EUR                    | SFCC                        |
| `ZimmermannEUIntl`         | `en-CH`                                       | `/en-ch/`                                  | EUR                    | Global-e                    |
| `ZimmermannHK`             | `en-HK`                                       | `/hk/`                                     | HKD (SFCC price books) | Global-e                    |
| `ZimmermannME`             | `en-AE`                                       | `/en-ae/`                                  | AED (SFCC price books) | Global-e                    |

- The site ID is resolved from the URL prefix on every request (SSR and CSR).
- AU is geo-redirected for non-Oceania human visitors; verified search bots and social unfurlers are exempt via UA allowlist.
- Per-environment SLAS client ID and SCAPI short code remain outstanding — see §11 item 2.

## 8. Failure modes and graceful degradation

| Failure                                       | Behaviour                                                                                                                                                                       |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| SLAS unavailable                              | Storefront cannot mint a guest token and is non-operational. Show a maintenance message. P1 incident.                                                                           |
| SCAPI catalogue 5xx                           | TanStack Query retries three times with exponential backoff. On final failure, show the last cached payload if available; otherwise show an error state with a "Try again" CTA. |
| SCAPI basket 5xx during add-to-cart           | Inline error toast. The user's intent stays in client state so a retry resends the same request.                                                                                |
| Order placement 5xx after Adyen authorisation | Hard error — the order cannot fail silently. The customer sees an explicit error with a contact reference and ops is alerted.                                                   |
| Einstein recommendations 5xx                  | Hide the slot or fall back to a static merchandising group.                                                                                                                     |
| SLAS token refresh fails                      | Force re-login. The basket is preserved on the guest token until the customer completes checkout.                                                                               |
| TSOB 409 (rapid storefront switch)            | Retry after 3 seconds. Do not re-login the customer — the existing session is still valid on the origin channel.                                                                |
| reCAPTCHA fails to load or token rejected     | Block the register/login submit, show a "please retry" message, and offer a contact-support path after two failures.                                                            |

## 9. Security and privacy

- All traffic is TLS 1.2+ over HTTPS.
- SLAS private-client flow — the authorisation code exchange is proxied through MRT so the client secret never reaches the browser.
- Refresh tokens are held in `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict` cookies — never in browser JavaScript.
- PCI scope is Adyen's — the browser sends payment data directly to Adyen. SFCC holds token references only.

## 10. Open items requiring client confirmation

1. **Login MFA scope.** Confirm whether multi-factor authentication on login is in scope for launch or post-launch. If in scope, the SLAS configuration and the PWA login flow need additional design.

2. **`sfPayments.metadataUrl` hostname.** The `sfcc-payments` undici connection pool (TSD §12.1) holds `config.app.sfPayments.metadataUrl`'s origin in a pool separate from `sfcc-scapi` (`{shortCode}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com`). That separation only provides blast-radius isolation if the two hosts are different origins. If `sfPayments.metadataUrl` resolves to the same SCAPI host, the pools should be merged.

name: Deploy Dev

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - develop

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  contract-tests:
    name: MuleSoft contract tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    continue-on-error: false
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install --include=dev

      # TODO: Replace with real contract assertion once MuleSoft publishes OpenAPI specs.
      # Owner: Zimmermann integration team + Accenture delivery lead to align.
      - name: Run contract tests
        run: npm run test:contracts

  bundle-size:
    name: Bundle size check
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    continue-on-error: false
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install --include=dev

      - name: Build and check bundle size
        run: npm run test:max-file-size

  dev-gate:
    name: Dev Gate
    needs: [contract-tests, bundle-size]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: always()
    steps:
      - name: Check all dev gate signals passed
        run: |
          if [ "${{ needs.contract-tests.result }}" != "success" ] || \
             [ "${{ needs.bundle-size.result }}" != "success" ]; then
            echo "Dev gate: one or more checks failed"
            echo "  contract-tests: ${{ needs.contract-tests.result }}"
            echo "  bundle-size:    ${{ needs.bundle-size.result }}"
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "Dev gate: all checks passed"

  deploy-dev:
    name: Deploy to dev
    needs: dev-gate
    if: needs.dev-gate.result == 'success'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: dev
    env:
      MRT_USER: ${{ secrets.MRT_USER }}
      MRT_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.MRT_API_KEY }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          cache: 'npm'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install --include=dev

      - name: Push build to dev
        run: npm run push:dev

  tag-sprint:
    name: Tag sprint rollover
    needs: dev-gate
    if: needs.dev-gate.result == 'success'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 2

      - name: Check for sprint.txt change
        id: sprint-check
        run: |
          if git diff HEAD~1 HEAD -- scripts/sprint.txt | grep -q .; then
            echo "changed=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "sprint=$(cat scripts/sprint.txt | tr -d '[:space:]')" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "changed=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          fi

      - name: Create sprint tag
        if: steps.sprint-check.outputs.changed == 'true'
        run: |
          SPRINT="${{ steps.sprint-check.outputs.sprint }}"
          TAG="sprint/${SPRINT}/$(date -u +%Y-%m-%d)"
          git tag "$TAG"
          git push origin "$TAG"
          echo "Tagged: $TAG"

content.text:
## Short answer: they're independent lanes, not a sequence

There is no single "deploy order" across the whole system. **PWA Kit doesn't deploy first or last relative to SFCC, Contentful, or MuleSoft/NewStore — it's just one of several separate, parallel deployment processes**, each with its own trigger, owner, and cadence.

I confirmed this by reading the actual CI file, not just the docs: [.github/workflows/deploy-dev.yml](.github/workflows/deploy-dev.yml) runs MuleSoft contract tests + a bundle-size check, then a single step — `npm run push:dev` — which pushes **only the MRT bundle**. That's it. There is no step in this repo's CI that deploys SFCC cartridges/config, no step that syncs Contentful, no step that touches MuleSoft. Each of those lives entirely outside this pipeline:

| Lane | How it deploys | Who triggers it | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PWA / MRT** | `npm run push:dev` (and equivalents per tier) | Automatic, on merge to `develop` (Dev tier); manual gate for Stage/UAT/Prod | This repo's `deploy-*.yml` |
| **SFCC Business Manager** | Cartridge code versions / site config import | A separate SFCC-side process, owned by Integration/SI partner — not driven by this repo's git branches at all | Not in this repo (per [[project_coverage_threshold]]-style split — it's a different backend repo/process) |
| **Contentful** | `npm run sync:contentful` (Management API, additive-only) | Manual, run on-demand by whoever added a content type | This repo, but **not wired into any `deploy-*.yml`** — you run it yourself |
| **MuleSoft / NewStore** | NewStore's own release cadence | Entirely owned by NewStore/Integration — a genuinely separate 2–3 month SIT cycle | Outside this repo entirely |

## The one place they *are* forced to line up

The diagram above shows it: **Stage** is the only documented convergence point. It won't open until *both* the Digital SIT Gate (the PWA's own CI checks) is green *and* NewStore has signed off its own SIT cycle. Below Stage, the four lanes genuinely don't wait on each other — that's explicitly by design (the Confluence topology page calls SIT "a parallel lane — it never gates the Digital release path").

## What does create a *practical* (not enforced) dependency

Nothing stops you from pushing new PWA code to a tier before the SFCC config or Contentful content it expects exists there — the deploy won't fail, the feature will just render empty/broken until the data shows up. A few concrete examples from the docs:

- A new Contentful content type's React component will render nothing useful until someone runs `npm run sync:contentful` **and** an editor populates an entry — neither is blocked or triggered by the PWA's own deploy.
- A PDP/PLP won't show real products in a given tier until that tier's SFCC sandbox actually has catalogue/pricebook data loaded — that's a separate SFCC/Business-Manager-side task (e.g. `SFCC-259..263` in Jira right now, loading catalogue/pricebook/inventory into UAT), independent of anything this repo pushes.
- Each MRT environment needs its own env vars (`COMMERCE_API_*`, `CONTENTFUL_*`, `MULESOFT_*`) configured once per tier (via `npm run env -- push <tier>`) before a push to that tier will actually work — but that's one-time setup, not a per-deploy ordering rule.

This is also consistent with AGENTS.md's **Graceful Degradation** principle — each integration is required to fail independently, precisely *because* nothing guarantees these lanes are in sync at any given moment.

**Bottom line for you as FED Lead:** if something looks broken in an environment, the first question isn't "did PWA deploy in the wrong order" — it's "which of the four independent lanes hasn't caught up yet" (stale Contentful sync, SFCC catalogue not loaded in that sandbox, MuleSoft/NewStore pointing at the wrong stub). That's a genuinely common failure mode with this architecture, not a deploy-sequencing bug.

content.text:
## Part 1 — How PWA Kit actually assembles a page

The very first diagram in this conversation showed the *who-talks-to-whom* map (PWA Kit → SFCC / Contentful / MuleSoft / 3rd-party). Here's the piece that was missing: **the order that happens in, for a single page load.**

1. **Browser requests a page** (e.g. a PDP URL).
2. **PWA Kit's server layer (running on MRT) does the work before anything reaches the browser.** This is Server-Side Rendering (SSR) — it's mandatory for product/category/content pages ([architecture.md §SSR Requirement](.docs/architecture.md:110)). At this point it fetches, **in parallel, not one-after-another**:
   - **SFCC** via SCAPI — product data, price, availability (`@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react`)
   - **Contentful** via the Delivery API — editorial content (banners, size guides)
   - **MuleSoft** (only for specific things like order history, stock checks — most pages don't need this)
3. **The server assembles a complete, already-rendered HTML page** and sends it to the browser — this is why a Zimmermann PDP is crawlable by Google and fast on first paint, unlike a pure client-side app that ships a blank shell.
4. **The browser "hydrates"** — React takes over the already-rendered HTML and makes it interactive, and then fetches personalised bits client-side (basket contents, logged-in customer info) since those can't be safely cached/rendered on the server for every visitor.
5. **Only after Didomi consent** does anything third-party load — GTM, Adyen's payment widget, Optimizely, etc. If consent state is unknown, none of it loads (fail-closed).

Cart, checkout, and My Account pages follow a lighter version of this: the shell (header/footer/layout) is still server-rendered, but the personal data (basket lines, order history) loads client-side after hydration rather than being baked into the server response — because that data is per-session and shouldn't be cached at the edge.

## Part 2 — Where the code physically lives, and how it becomes a live URL

All Zimmermann-specific code lives in `overrides/`, mirroring the structure of the unmodified `@salesforce/retail-react-app` package pulled in from npm — you never edit `node_modules/` directly; your override file just takes precedence at build time.

The diagram above shows the actual mechanics, verified against the real scripts in [package.json](package.json:76) rather than just the docs:

1. **Write code** in `overrides/`.
2. **`npm run build`** — runs `pwa-kit-dev build`, which is Webpack 5 producing `build/main.js`, `build/vendor.js`, and the SSR server bundle.
3. **`pwa-kit-dev push -t <tier>`** — uploads that bundle to Salesforce's Managed Runtime for the target environment (`dev`/`sit`/`staging`/`uat`/`production`). By default, **pushing also activates it immediately** — there's no separate manual "go live" click for a normal deploy.
4. **Live on CDN** — the activated bundle is what actually answers requests, sitting behind a CDN (Akamai by default) that handles TLS and edge caching in front of the MRT Node process doing the SSR work from Part 1.

**Rollback works differently from a redeploy:** MRT keeps a history of bundles (10 for SIT, 50 bundles / ~30-day window for Prod), so reverting a bad release doesn't mean rebuilding and re-pushing old code — it means re-activating a bundle that's already sitting there: `mrt:activate --target production --bundle-id <PREVIOUS_ID>`. That's the fastest recovery path, faster than any CI re-run.

**One honest gap, verified just now, not assumed:** `pwa-kit-dev push` needs `mobify.config.js` to know the project slug and which MRT environment each tier alias (`dev`, `sit`, etc.) actually points to. I checked — **that file doesn't exist in the repo yet** (`ls mobify.config.js` → no such file, and it's never been committed per `git log`). So as of right now, if someone ran `npm run push:dev` today, it would fail before it got anywhere near MRT. This is tracked, known work (it's listed as a Tier 1 file to be owned by Integration/SI partner once created), not a hidden landmine — but it means the deploy pipeline as drawn is the *intended* mechanism, and the only leg of it actually exercised so far is CI's automatic Dev push, which itself depends on this file existing.

Let's slow way down. Here's your mental model, mapped 1:1:

| Your simple site | Zimmermann's site |
|---|---|
| Frontend repo (React) | PWA Kit (also React) |
| Frontend hosted on **Vercel** | PWA Kit hosted on **MRT** (Managed Runtime) |
| Backend repo (your own API) | **There isn't one you write.** SFCC plays that role instead |
| Backend hosted on **Railway** | SFCC isn't hosted by this team at all — it's Salesforce's own always-on service, like calling Stripe's or Shopify's API |
| "Push backend first, so frontend has something to call" | **Doesn't apply.** SFCC is already running 24/7 whether or not anyone ever touches this repo |

The one real difference from your setup: in your example, *you* write and deploy both sides. Here, this team only ever writes and deploys **one side — PWA Kit**. Everything it talks to (SFCC, Contentful, MuleSoft) belongs to a different company and is already running, all the time, independent of this repo.

**The four things, as simply as possible:**

- **PWA Kit** — the actual website code (React). The only thing "your repo" builds.
- **MRT** — where that code runs once deployed. Not quite plain static hosting like Vercel for a pure frontend — it also runs a small Node server (that's the "Node application" part), whose job is to fetch data *before* the page reaches the browser, and to keep secret API keys off the browser.
- **SFCC** — the product catalogue, prices, cart, orders. Already running, owned by Salesforce. PWA Kit just asks it questions ("what's this product's price?").
- **Contentful** — "what does this page actually say" — banners, homepage layout, size guides. Also already running, owned by Contentful. PWA Kit asks it "what content goes here today?"
- **MuleSoft** — a translator sitting behind SFCC. A few older backend systems (order management, loyalty, CRM) don't speak SFCC's language, so MuleSoft passes messages between them. PWA Kit barely talks to it directly — mostly just for things like order history.
- **3rd-party / direct** — scripts that skip all of the above and just run straight in the customer's browser (payment widget, chat bubble, analytics). Simplest of the four.

**How one page actually gets built, in order:**

1. Customer's browser asks for a page.
2. PWA Kit's Node server (on MRT) asks SFCC ("what's the price?") and Contentful ("what's the content?") **at the same time**.
3. It combines both answers into one finished page and sends it down.
4. The browser turns that into a working React app.
5. A few extra scripts (3rd-party) load directly in the browser — unrelated to steps 2-3.
6. MuleSoft only shows up on specific pages (like order history), not every page.

**So — does the "backend" deploy first?**

No, because nothing backend-shaped ever deploys here. SFCC / Contentful / MuleSoft just... exist, running, regardless of what this repo does. The only "deploy" in this whole picture is pushing PWA Kit's code to MRT. What *does* need to be ready first isn't a deploy — it's **data**: SFCC needs products loaded, Contentful needs content filled in. But that's someone typing into an admin screen, not a code push.

2. Bigger nuance you're missing: **MuleSoft isn't only reached via SFCC.** PWA Kit's own Node layer (on MRT) calls MuleSoft **directly**, completely bypassing SFCC, for a specific set of read-only things: order history, order details, boutique/stock checks, and GiveX balance check. - For a normal content block (say, a homepage banner or size guide), **Contentful supplies the ingredients only** — this image, this headline text, this link — and the PWA Kit *component code* is the actual recipe: it decides how those ingredients get arranged, styled, and displayed. Contentful has no idea what the banner will look like.

# 02 — Contentful (CMS)

## 1. Purpose and scope

Contentful is the headless CMS for editorial content: homepage modules, promotional banners, lookbooks, campaign landing pages, size guide fallback content (primary size guide is the Measmerize overlay — PRD-053), footer, and editorial blocks on PLPs and PDPs. The storefront reads published content via the **Delivery API (CDA)** from both SSR and the browser, reads draft content via the **Preview API (CPA)** in editor sessions, and receives **publish webhooks** to clear the SSR cache.

In scope:

- Reading published content via the Delivery API
- Reading draft content via the Preview API in editor preview sessions
- Live preview in Contentful Studio
- Locale-specific content via Contentful's native localisation
- Contentful Studio Experiences — drag-and-drop page composition by editors
- Receiving publish webhooks to clear stale SSR cache entries

Out of scope of this document:

- Content type schema sync (managed in code via the Management API — see §2)
- Asset uploads and content editing in Contentful Studio
- Webhooks from Contentful to SFCC (none planned)

**Content ownership.** SFCC owns all commerce data; Contentful owns editorial. On pages that mix both, editorial comes from Contentful and commerce data is resolved from SFCC. Product and category references in Contentful entries are authored via the Salesforce Commerce Cloud Connector app and resolved at render (HPC-001). Rows marked *pending* are unconfirmed (see §11).

| Surface | SFCC owns | Contentful owns | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Homepage | Commerce data for embedded product refs | All modules — hero, banners, campaign blocks | Confirmed |
| Campaign landing pages | Commerce data for embedded product refs | Full page (Contentful Studio Experiences) | Confirmed |
| Lookbooks | Commerce data for shop-the-look refs | Imagery, layout, copy | Confirmed |
| Size guides | — | Fallback content only — primary size guide is the Measmerize overlay (PRD-053, confirmed 2026-06-19); Contentful serves size guide content only where no Measmerize data exists for a given product | Updated |
| Footer | — | All content | Confirmed |
| PLP / category | Category results, product tiles, facets, pagination, hero/banner and editorial rows (SFCC BM — SPR-03/04/64) | Contentful-authored editorial rows, if any | *Whether any PLP editorial comes from Contentful is pending* |
| PDP | Product attributes, price, inventory, variations, gallery | Marketing copy, editorial blocks, size guide fallback (primary size guide is Measmerize — PRD-053) | *Which blocks are Contentful vs SFCC Page Designer is pending* |
| Navigation / mega-menu | Category tree | Promotional tiles, if any | *Pending* |
| Product badges | Badge labels and taxonomy — managed in SFCC BM product attributes (PRD-005); clickable badges link to category/PLP. Contentful is not the source of badge content unless explicitly confirmed. | — | Confirmed |

## 2. Content type management (build-time)

Content type schemas are managed in code, not in the Contentful UI:

- Schema definitions live in the PWA repo and are reviewed via pull request.
- A sync script (Management API) idempotently upserts content types into the target environment. The sync script is authored to be additive only — it never deletes a field from a live content type.
- Each content type pairs with a typed React component. TypeScript types match the Contentful field IDs exactly, so schema drift is caught at compile time.

## 3. Browser-side architecture

```
PWA (SSR layer, then CSR hydration)
        │
        ├──► Contentful Delivery API (CDA) — published content
        │        SSR fetches server-side; browser also uses CDA on
        │        post-hydration reads. Public token, safe in bundle.
        │
        ├──► Contentful Preview API (CPA) — draft content
        │        Editor preview only. Token held server-side in MRT;
        │        never reaches the browser. Requests proxied through
        │        an MRT preview endpoint.
        │
        ├──► Contentful Images API (images.ctfassets.net)
        │        srcset / sizes / avif|webp / quality parameters
        │
        └──◄  Publish webhook → MRT /webhooks/contentful
                 Clears affected SSR cache keys on entry publish.
                 HMAC-verified with a shared secret.
```

- **SSR first.** Editorial content for SEO- and LCP-critical pages (homepage, PLP, PDP, campaign landings) is fetched server-side. The browser hydrates from the SSR payload — no CDA call on first paint.
- **GraphQL for composed pages.** Where a page assembles many entries the storefront uses the GraphQL Content API to fetch only the needed fields in one request. REST CDA is used for simpler reads.
- **Live preview.** When an editor opens preview in Contentful Studio, the storefront renders inside Studio's iframe. It detects the preview origin, switches to the CPA-backed MRT proxy, and refreshes on `postMessage` events from Studio.
- **Asset delivery.** Images come from `images.ctfassets.net`. The storefront generates `srcset`, `sizes`, AVIF with WebP fallback, and quality parameters per breakpoint.

## 4. Authentication and credentials

| Token | Where used | Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery API token (CDA) | Browser bundle and SSR | Public — read-only, scoped to one environment. Safe to embed. |
| Preview API token (CPA) | MRT preview proxy only | Semi-sensitive — exposes drafts. MRT environment variable. Never reaches the browser. |
| Management API token (CMA) | Build-time schema sync script | High. Held on the CI host only. Never embedded. |
| Webhook shared secret | MRT webhook receiver | High. Verifies HMAC on inbound publish webhooks. MRT environment variable. |

Each environment has its own CDA, CPA, and webhook-secret values. The CMA token is per-Space and held only on the CI host.

## 5. Data exchanged

| Direction | Data | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Storefront → Contentful | Content type ID, locale, filters, GraphQL query | CDA / Preview API HTTPS GET |
| Contentful → Storefront | JSON entries with resolved linked references | CDA / Preview API response |
| Contentful → Storefront (assets) | Image and video asset URLs | Images API |
| Contentful Studio ↔ PWA iframe | Live preview update events | Cross-origin `postMessage` |
| Contentful → MRT | Publish webhook with entry ID, content type, locale, environment | HTTPS POST with HMAC signature |

No PII flows through Contentful.

## 6. Performance and loading strategy

- **SSR cache.** Contentful responses are cached at the SSR/edge layer — TTL 60 seconds with stale-while-revalidate. Publish webhooks clear the cache; the TTL is the fallback.
- **CDN rate limits.** Contentful allows 55 uncached requests per second per CDA token. The SSR cache absorbs almost all traffic so this limit is only a risk during burst republish events.
- **Images.** AVIF with WebP fallback via the Images API. Lazy loading on all below-the-fold images. The largest hero carries `fetchpriority="high"`.
- **Preconnect.** `images.ctfassets.net` is preconnected from the document head. `cdn.contentful.com` is not — first paint hydrates from SSR, so no browser CDA call is on the critical path.
- **Bundle weight.** The rich-text renderer is dynamically imported only on pages that use rich-text fields.
- **Field projection.** GraphQL queries select only the fields the component uses. REST queries use the `select` parameter where supported.

## 7. Multi-region behaviour

- A single Contentful Space serves all eight storefronts via Contentful's native locale model.
- The active locale is resolved from the URL prefix and passed as `locale=` on every CDA request. Eleven active locales: en-AU, en-US, en-GB, en (EU), fr, it, es, en-CH, en-HK, en-AE.
- Region-specific entries (banners, promotions, editorial that varies by site) are filtered at query time using the active SFCC site ID.

## 8. Failure modes and graceful degradation

| Failure | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Contentful CDA unavailable | Page renders without editorial content. Editorial slots show empty; commerce data is never blocked on a CMS read. |
| Stale cached content after a publish | Tolerated within the 60-second TTL. The publish webhook normally clears affected entries in seconds; the TTL is the safety net if the webhook drops. |
| Preview API returns broken or unpublished refs | Editor preview only — render a placeholder. Production traffic never hits this path. |
| Asset (image) 404 | Show alt text and a graceful placeholder. |
| 429 rate limit on CDA | Exponential backoff and retry. The SSR cache makes this rare in practice. |
| Publish webhook fails HMAC verification | Reject and log. Storefront continues serving from cache; the TTL picks up the change. |
| Live preview iframe disconnects | Storefront silently returns to non-preview mode. |

## 9. Security and privacy

- The CDA token is read-only and scoped to one environment. Embedding in the bundle is safe per Contentful's published guidance.
- The CPA token is held server-side only and is never logged.
- The CMA token is held only on the CI host — never embedded, never in PR diffs.
- No PII is handled by Contentful.

## 10. Open items requiring client confirmation

1. **`regions` content-model field.** The working assumption is that region-specific entries are filtered by a `regions` field containing the relevant SFCC site IDs. Pending content-strategy and editor-workflow sign-off — this field affects how editors author content across all eight storefronts.
2. **SFCC vs Contentful content ownership on composed pages.** The principle is settled — SFCC owns all commerce data, Contentful owns editorial. Not yet confirmed is the split on composed pages: which editorial blocks appear on PDP and PLP, whether they are authored in SFCC Page Designer or Contentful, whether category landing pages are SFCC-routed or built in Contentful Studio Experiences, and whether the mega-menu includes Contentful-authored promotional tiles. The working assumption is in the ownership table in §1.
3. **Contentful Space and per-environment credentials.** Contentful to provide per-environment CDA token, CPA token, Space ID, environment ID, and webhook secret so the storefront can be tested against a real Contentful environment.

content.thinking: I need to look at the HotspotPopup component to understand how it retrieves product data from SFCC, and then check the experience page renderer to see how it fetches the Contentful entry and wires up the component definitions for the layout.

I've found the complete picture here — the content type schema gets defined in code and synced to Contentful through the Management API, then the React component receives those Contentful fields as props (the image, alt text, and hotspots data as JSON) and renders the interactive layout.

The registration step in `definitions.ts` is where the blueprint concept actually lives — it tells Contentful Studio which components are available for editors to drag onto pages and what fields each one needs. The page fetch route then ties it all together by taking a URL slug, instantiating a Contentful client with the appropriate token, and calling the SDK's fetch function to retrieve the Experience entry matching that slug.

The real magic happens when HotspotMarker connects to HotspotPopup — it takes just a `productId` string from Contentful's JSON and uses the SFCC commerce SDK hook to fetch live product data (price, name, image) directly from SFCC. This is the concrete example of how a single component blends Contentful-sourced positioning and product references with real-time SFCC product information.

There's also a distinction between simple content-type components like HeroBanner (where a container fetches the entry and passes fields as props) versus Experience Builder components (registered globally and composed by editors in Studio, then rendered generically by ExperienceRoot). The Experience Builder flow is the more complete answer to how layout mapping works, since it shows the full composition system rather than just standard content type usage.

I should also clarify the product data flow — products for normal display come directly from SFCC via the commerce SDK, not through MuleSoft or NewStore. MuleSoft and NewStore are specifically for real-time stock and BOPIS availability checks, plus order history.
